title: Asset tokenization, 24x5 markets and the T+0 end-state
snippet: An in-depth analysis of the strategic significance of tokenization and its role in enabling banks, asset managers and asset-servicing ecosystems to operate with greater continuity, precision and control.
fullText:
Executive summary

Asset tokenization has entered a new phase. No longer a peripheral innovation theme associated primarily with crypto-token ecosystems, it is becoming embedded in the core architecture of regulated capital markets. Three developments make this clear: First, Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation’s (DTCC) December 2025 tokenization initiative established a credible regulatory pathway for tokenized recording of security entitlements inside the US markets’ central post-trade infrastructure. Second, London Stock Exchange Group’s (LSEG) July 2026 ‘LSE 24’ announcement signaled that major exchanges are redesigning market access around new-continuous, algorithmic and globally distributed trading activity. Third, the industry-wide drive toward T+0 (or ‘near-real-time’) settlement is placing new pressure on institutions to eliminate operational latency, manual breaks and fragmented controls models across the transaction lifecycle.

Taken together, these developments point to a structural shift in financial industry operating models. The implication is not that tokenization will replace existing market infrastructures in the near term. It is rather that tokenization is emerging as one of the few credible mechanisms for synchronizing ownership data, transfer logic, collateral status, tax attributes, lifecycle events and reporting obligations across an increasingly time-compressed market environment.

For executive leadership teams, this is an enterprise transformation issue rather than a product innovation topic. CIOs should assess tokenization through the lens of portfolio utility rather than technological novelty. For CFOs it would be advantageous to view tokenization through the lenses of liquidity efficiency, cost-to-serve and balance-sheet velocity. COOs should recognize it as an opportunity to optimize lifecycle ownership, exception management and operating resilience. For CROs the main objective would be to preserve controls effectiveness as the operating model becomes faster and more distributed. CTOs should treat it as an interoperability, control and data architecture foundation for the future. Tax, legal and compliance leaders should now place more priority on the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework (CARF), which is beginning to shape how tokenized workflows must be clarified, evidenced and reported across jurisdictions.

The central thesis of this whitepaper is straightforward. The strategic significance of tokenization does not lie in digitizing instruments for its own sake. It lies rather in enabling banks, asset managers and asset-servicing ecosystems to operate with greater continuity, precision and control as trading hours extend, settlement cycles compress, and regulatory expectations become more data-intensive. Institutions that act now can shape optimized target operating models, while the rules are still being defined. Those that wait risk becoming ‘takers’ of market structures defined by others.

A structural inflection point

The financial industry has spent the last decade improving the speed of market access while leaving much of the post-trade chain fundamentally sequential. Trading stacks became faster, more automated and more globally distributed, yet settlement, servicing, transfer controls and tax and regulatory reporting often remained dependent on cutoffs, manual interventions and multiple layers of message-based reconciliations. That model was sustainable in a world defined by discrete market windows and settlement cycles long enough to absorb operational ambiguity. However, it becomes fundamentally less resilient – to the point of being clearly inadequate – in a world characterized by 24x5 trading markets 4, compressed settlement timescales 8 and higher regulatory expectations 9 around data quality and reporting standards.

This is why the December 2025 DTCC development 123 matters. DTC’s SEC staff no-action relief did not merely authorize another industry pilot. It also validated the proposition that tokenized assets can sit alongside the core infrastructure of regulated securities markets without undermining established legal frameworks or settled market practices. That point has broad strategic significance: once tokenization is anchored inside regulated post-trade mechanisms, it then moves from conceptual possibility to mandated operating-model option.

LSEG’s ‘LSE 24’ announcement 456 carries similar weight, albeit from a different angle. By extending weekday market access towards near-continuous trading, LSEG is effectively signaling that historical assumptions about acceptable market hours, operational handoffs, surveillance windows and servicing timetables can, and eventually will, be challenged. Of course, this does not by itself constitute a mandate for tokenization. It does, however, intensify the commercial and operational need for infrastructures that can maintain persistent state and control integrity beyond traditional market windows.

The push towards T+0 settlement 789 is the third force completing the picture. Across jurisdictions, policy and market direction continue to favor shorter settlement cycles, higher automation, lower frictions and improved liquidity usage. Yet, T+0 at scale would not be primarily a messaging problem, but rather an intraday liquidity, control and synchronization one. Financial institutions cannot settle faster simply by accelerating instructions; they must also establish real-time certainty on asset availability, beneficial ownership, transfer eligibility, collateral sufficiency, tax treatment and exception status. Tokenization then becomes strategically relevant, as it offers a path to representing more aspects of concrete lifecycle states in a synchronized, consistent and machine-processable form.

Why are these developments converging now?

A narrow reading of current market developments would treat DTCC tokenization, LSE 24 and T+0 roadmaps as parallel but separate trends. That would be missing the point: each and every one of said developments increases the value proposition of the other two.

DTCC’s initiative increases the institutional credibility of tokenization by bringing it inside the perimeter of regulated U.S. post-trade infrastructures. LSE 24 increases the business value of synchronized post-trade outcomes because around-the-clock trading extends market depth, under the proviso that books, controls and follow-on entitlements remain coherent. The T+0 settlement imperative increases the urgency of transaction lifecycle redesign, as the tolerance for breaks, re-keying and batch-based exception handling will decline sharply across market participants and regulators alike.

The resulting strategic calculation is clear: tokenization is emerging as not simply a workflow around a new asset format, but rather as an operating infrastructure for compressed market lifecycles 13810. In practical terms, that means that tokenization should be assessed less on whether it creates a novel client proposition, and more on whether it reduces reconciliation drag, improves collateral mobility, sharpens intraday balance-sheet visibility, strengthens value transfer controls and lowers the cost of accurate tax and regulatory reporting.

This calculation is especially important for senior management. Many financial institutions continue to evaluate tokenization in the same governance forums as those tasked with digital-asset experimentation and broader technical innovation. That approach is simply too narrow. The more relevant framing would be to evaluate it as enterprise-level change spanning client-facing, market infrastructure, custody, servicing, tax, risk and data management units. Once approached in that way, tokenization ceases to be a speculative technology agenda point and occupies its true space as a board-level, strategic business model question.

Jurisdictional outlook

United States and North America

The December 2025 SEC staff no-action relief granted to the Depository Trust Company (DTC) is the defining U.S. development in scope. It authorizes a limited, voluntary pilot in which participants may elect to have claims to DTC-held securities registered using distributed ledger technology rather than only through DTC’s traditional (i.e. centralized) ledger. DTCC subsequently confirmed in May 2026 that more than 50 firms had joined development efforts around this service, reinforcing the perception that the initiative is not a theoretical exercise but an ecosystem development program with broad market resonance.

The significance of this development extends beyond the pilot itself. It demonstrates that regulated incumbents are willing to incorporate tokenized representations of value in existing legal and operational frameworks 1415. That should eventually lower the adoption threshold for still other banks, custodians and asset managers, because the choice is no longer between legacy infrastructure and an entirely new market model; it is rather between remaining fragmented and moving towards synchronized coexistence.

From a North American perspective (due to osmosis with the US ecosystem), the broader message is that tokenization will be judged through post-trade economics, resilience and scalability outcomes, rather than through crypto-market rhetoric. That is a more consequential test, and for established financial institutions and other market participants, a more investable one.

United Kingdom

LSEG’s July 2026 LSE 24 announcement has strategic importance well beyond its initial product scope. The LSE 24 venue is intended to operate separately from the Main Market, offer near-continuous weekday trading, commence client testing by the end of 2026 and launch with exchange traded products (ETPs) in the first half of 2027 (subject to regulatory approval). That signals a willingness by one of the world’s major exchanges to redesign market participation around globally distributed, machine-driven activity.

The implication in a UK context is clear. Once trading extends beyond conventional windows, financial institutions must reassess eligibility, order management, pre-funding, custody operations, settlement dependencies, surveillance reports, tax-lot continuity and corporate-action mechanisms and associated controls. This creates a strong pull towards more persistent, machine-processable asset representations and more automated post-trade control frameworks. In this respect, LSE 24 should be understood less as an isolated extended-market-hours initiative and more as a catalyst for operating model modernization.

The UK is also relevant in the CARF 1112 context, because it is among the jurisdictions moving early on implementation timing. This increases pressure on financial institutions to design tokenized operating models with embedded residency, account-linkage and reporting logic from the outset.

European Union

The EU already has a formal legal framework for tokenized financial market infrastructures through the DLT Pilot Regime. Since March 2023, said regime has provided the basis for DLT multilateral trading facilities, DLT settlement systems and integrated trading-settlement systems under a controlled exemption model. In April 2026, the European Commission explicitly linked tokenization to reduced payment and settlement frictions, improved liquidity management, programmability potential and streamlined reconciliation, while also signaling that the framework would need broadening if EU digital markets are to achieve meaningful scale and competitiveness.

This is a significant policy marker. The EU is no longer debating whether tokenized securities belong inside regulated markets. The debate has already shifted to how quickly the framework can evolve from experimentation to institutionalization without undermining investor protection, MiFID II discipline or market integrity. For EU banks and asset managers, the practical opportunity lies in use cases where process frictions are already substantial: UCITS funds, bonds, collateral pools, trade finance, subscription credit facilities, transfer restrictions and cross-border servicing.

CARF adds a further layer of complexity because the EU’s broader reporting and transparency agenda is increasingly intolerant towards ambiguous asset classification and fragmented intermediation chains. As tokenized instruments sit closer to the boundaries between securities, crypto-assets and digitally transferable claims, institutions will need sharper classification, stronger data lineage and more robust governance over reporting consequences.

Switzerland

Switzerland continues to occupy an important position as a reference jurisdiction for tokenized rights. The Federal Council and the State Secretariat for International Finance describe 1617 the Swiss distributed ledger technology (DLT) legal framework (effective from August 2021) as creating legal certainty for tokenized assets, enabling ledger-based securities and allowing for licensed DLT trading facilities. In addition, in October 2025 Swiss authorities opened consultation on amendments intended to improve market growth potential and integrate innovative financial technologies, while safeguarding market integrity and investor protection.

For international financial institutions, Switzerland’s significance is anchored not only in fintech reputation, but, more significantly, in legal certainty. It provides a practical model for embedding tokenization into mainstream private-law and market-infrastructure architectures. This is highly relevant to institutions seeking to test novel issuance, transfer control, custody and distribution models within a welcoming environment with comparatively mature legal clarity.

Switzerland also matters for cross-border wealth and booking models interacting with CARF-implementing jurisdictions. Even where Swiss law provides clean recognition of tokenized rights, internationally active financial institutions still need aligned client, residency, asset-classification and transaction-lineage data to support downstream reporting and tax transparency obligations. Robustness of regulatory disclosures (also as a first-base position from which to manage regulatory risk) will of course follow.

Singapore

Singapore has positioned itself as one of the most prominent institutional tokenization hubs in Asia. Moneytary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has published a Guide on the Tokenisation of Capital Markets Products 18, clarifying how securities laws and related legislation apply to tokenized capital markets products and to the entities facilitating their issuance and intermediation. MAS has also advanced practical operating models of tokenization through project ‘Guardian’ and related work on tokenized funds 19.

Singapore’s strategic importance lies in the way it combines legal clarity with supervisory expectations of production-grade operating controls. For banks and asset managers, it is a strong jurisdiction in which to test tokenized funds, digitally native servicing models, tokenized collateral mobility and cross-border distribution arrangements without worrying if regulatory ambiguity will influence the market acceptance of robust token ecosystem designs.

Singapore is also relevant from a CARF perspective. Its active regulatory support for asset tokenization, combined with its commitment to implement CARF, reinforces the importance for financial institutions of developing robust tax residency, client identity, transaction attribution and wallet-account linkage capabilities, which support both regulatory reporting and participation in regulated tokenized markets.

Hong Kong SAR

Hong Kong has also taken meaningful steps forward towards asset tokenization. On 20 April 2026, the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) issued a circular on the tokenization of SFC-authorised investment products 2021 which sets out detailed conditions relating to disclosure, primary market dealing, secondary trading, operational soundness, record keeping, cybersecurity, smart-contract integrity, business continuity, legal prerequisites and prior-consultation practices. This level of specificity makes Hong Kong SAR one of the clearest examples of a regulatory jurisdiction moving from conceptual openness to actionable supervisory expectations.

Hong Kong is therefore particularly relevant for institutional product manufacturers and platform operators. It can be argued that it leads the way in demonstrating what an effective supervisory framework for asset tokenization at scale could look like in practice. It also underscores a broader market truth, namely that tokenization is not reducing the need for controls, but rather re-assigning and (at least partially) intensifying them.

Although Hong Kong’s CARF implementation timeline may lag the earliest wave, internationally active financial institutions should not interpret this as a reason to defer framework readiness. Cross-border distribution models and multi-jurisdictional asset servicing chains will still require high-quality tax-relevant data capture and classification from transaction inception.

India

Today, India still remains more significant as an asset distribution, servicing and tax-reporting jurisdiction than as a mature institutional tokenized securities hub. Official tax guidance 22 confirms the taxation of virtual digital assets and relevant withholding/reporting obligations, including references to reporting requirements for specified entities. Draft-rule developments in 2026 23 also indicate a widening of the tax reporting perimeter to cryptoassets and related digital products.

The practical message is clear: in India, reporting and taxation considerations may end-up shaping tokenized business models before capital-market regulations do. Any asset structure touching India-nexus clients, distribution, taxable events or local intermediation should therefore be assessed primarily through classification robustness, transaction-level traceability and reporting repercussions. For many financial institutions, this will probably influence where products are booked, which investor groups are targeted and how cross-border platforms are designed.

Japan

Japan is strategically important for the value proposition of asset tokenization, because it couples sophisticated financial regulation with comparatively advanced CARF implementation initiatives. Japanese domestic CARF requirements took effect from 1 January 2026 24, so that affected entities are already obliged to verify tax residence and submit annual reports on covered activities. Importantly, updated interpretative material 25 has addressed the treatment of electronically recorded transferable rights representing securities, clarifying that said rights are treated as cryptoassets for CARF purposes only when they also have the characteristics of cryptoassets under the Payment Services Act.

This distinction is highly significant. It shows that tokenized securities in Japan do not automatically self-classify with respect to CARF, their classification rather depending on their actual legal and functional characteristics. For financial institutions designing products across jurisdictions, this means that rights analysis, asset structuring, transfer logic, and custody design can all influence token classification, and by extension determine tax-reporting obligations. Japan therefore provides one of the clearest examples of why asset tokenization initiatives must be governed by multi-disciplinary business, operations, legal, tax and technology teams.

Cross-jurisdictional legal signals

In our estimation, court-led precedent remains less developed than regulatory guidance in the area of asset tokenization. The implication is important: throughout 2025 and 2026, the area’s operative legal architecture was being built primarily through no-action relief, circulars, statutory frameworks, supervisory guides and tax FAQs rather than through a deep body of jurisdictional case law. Financial institutions should therefore assign these tokenized instruments the same attention they would traditionally reserve for assets under still evolving (and not settled) judicial doctrines.

Tokenized workflow risks and opportunities

Cross-ledger interoperability

Cross-ledger interoperability is becoming a decisive design requirement 26 as tokenized markets move from isolated pilots to production ecosystems. The core issue is no longer whether a digital representation of value is allowed to exist on a distributed ledger; it is rather whether assets, liquidity, collateral, identity and reporting data can move coherently across multiple (centralized and distributed) ledgers, networks and service providers without introducing reconciliation breaks or legal ambiguities.

For banks, interoperability has three dimensions. The first is technical: standards, APIs, smart-contract logic, identity frameworks and message formats must support transferability across venues and infrastructures. The second is operational: settlement, custody, collateral management, treasury and compliance processes must be able to consume and validate state from more than one ledger without duplicating risk controls 27. The third is legal: firms must know which ledger is authoritative for ownership, settlement finality, pledges, control transfers and reporting-relevant classifications – and in which jurisdiction 29.

This matters because tokenized markets are already fragmenting across public chains, permissioned networks, CSD-centered infrastructures and bank-owned internal ledgers. The ECB, for example, has explicitly identified 33 platform fragmentation as one of the main obstacles to digital asset scale, and it has framed interoperability and shared standards as central building blocks of the EU’s tokenized financial market architecture.

Industry initiatives around digital asset securities interoperability further indicate that market participants are converging on the same conclusion: without a common interoperability layer, tokenization risks recreating the very silos it was meant to eliminate.

The original strategic argument is that interoperability is the hidden prerequisite for every other tokenization use case. T+0 settlement cannot operate across fragmented ledgers unless asset rights state, liquidity state and collateral state can all be trusted to be accurate across systems in real time. Likewise, CARF reporting becomes materially harder when transaction data is split across multiple networks, cross-ledgers, and intermediate service providers. Interoperability is therefore not a back-office engineering concern, it is rather a stakeholder-level (and sponsor-level approved) design specification for a robust and sustainable tokenized finance business model.

For senior executives, the practical response should be to define an interoperability strategy before scaling production. That strategy should answer four questions, namely: Which ledgers, or networks, are to be in-scope? Which blockchain layer is to be the authoritative one for ownership and settlement finality? How are identity and reporting data to be normalized across networks? And which interoperability or platform layer (bridge, roll-up, oracle or other) is to orchestrate value and state transfers, collateral mobility and valuation signals, and finally exception handling across the target ecosystem?

Custody risk management in T+0 settlements

Custody risk management becomes materially more important as accepted settlement standards compress towards T+0. The traditional custody model benefited from built-in time buffers: at total buffer was providing time to affirm standing settlement instructions, source securities, mobilize collateral, investigate breaks, validate corporate-action status and repair mismatches, all before final settlement could crystallize. In a T+0 setting, that allowed time buffer shrinks sharply. The custody function therefore moves from a largely post-trade paradigm to an intraday risk-orchestration one 2731.

This has four strategic consequences.

First, asset structure and rights certainty become critical control objectives. Custodians and their clients must know, with far greater detail than traditionally expected, which legal entity owns what, where it is held, whether it is available to settle, whether it is encumbered, and whether any transfer restrictions or servicing events affect availability. Tokenized asset models may help 30 by making both structure and rights more visible (ascertainable), but only if legal ownership, ledger design and custody records remain demonstrably aligned.

Second, operational resilience may be re-engineered around intraday exception management. In T+1 and longer settlement settings, many custody breaks can be escalated and repaired after the trading session ends. In T+0, however, unresolved SSI issues, mismatched account selections, incomplete tax attributes, sanctions hits, corporate-action ambiguities or ledger reconciliation breaks can all translate almost immediately to settlement failures – and potentially to emergency funding requests 31. Custody operating models will therefore need higher automation, pre-validation and live observability mechanisms.

Third, collateral and liquidity controls become inseparable from custody ones. Shorter settlement windows reduce counterparty exposures in principle, but they also reduce the time available to source liquidity, substitute collateral, meet margin calls or resolve failed allocations. Recent industry commentary 28 has pointed out that accelerated settlement can lower exposures, albeit while raising short-term liquidity and operational risks if supporting controls lag behind market latencies. This means that custodians, triparty agents, treasury teams and clearing functions must all operate against a much more tightly synchronized intraday view of inventory, collateral eligibility and funding capacity.

Fourth, digital assets and tokenized custody both introduce new control domains that traditional custody teams do not always own today. Private-key governance, wallet-account linkage, smart-contract dependency management, blockchain node or network resilience and cross-ledger reconciliation all become intertwined and relevant 32 once tokenized assets enter production workflows. These are not reasons to reject tokenization, they are rather reasons to elevate custody architecture, governance and controls testing to the level of operational cornerstones before scaling tokenized T+0 use cases.

The executive implication is clear: for boards, CIOs, COOs and heads of custody, T+0 should be treated as a custody transformation agenda as much as a settlement initiative. Financial institutions that accelerate settlement without re-designing custody controls will be simply shifting risk from end-of-day processing events to intraday liquidity events, servicing failures and evidentiary gaps. Whereas those that strengthen custody risk management will be able to leverage T+0 settlement capabilities to strengthen their competitive resilience posture.

A robust custody risk management program for tokenized and accelerated settlement markets should include at least six priorities:

    

Tokenized assets registry, common across custodians, sub-custodians, CSDs, wallets and internal books

    

Pre-trade and pre-settlement validation of SSIs, account eligibility, encumbrance status, watchlist controls (on both transaction participants and collateral) and tax attributes

    

Intraday reconciliation across tokenized asset ledgers, traditional books and external infrastructures

    

Explicit governance arrangements over private keys, wallet operations, recovery processes and smart contract change management (where tokenized assets are involved)

    

Tight integration of custody, treasury, collateral management and securities-financing functions

    

Escalation playbooks for intraday breaks, including fail prevention, fallback settlement and client communication protocols.

In short, the practical question to answer will be not whether T+0 is effective in isolation, but whether the custody model can also carry the subsequent operational load without creating new failure points. The institutions most likely to succeed will be those that treat custody as the ultimate T+0 control system, rather than as a passive post-trade ‘consumer’.

The CARF perspective

CARF 13 can be mistaken for being simply a tax-reporting overlay. Such a view would be severely incomplete. In practice, CARF has the hallmarks of becoming a design parameter of tokenized operating models. By requiring the reporting and exchange of information on certain crypto-asset transactions, it increases the strategic value of being able to leverage high-quality token classification, transaction lineage and participant identifier data.

Its expected influence on the success of asset tokenization can be grouped into four areas.

First, CARF forces financial institutions to be systematic and disciplined in classifying tokenized instruments. The more the use of tokenized securities, fund units, digitally transferable claims and other crypto-assets converges in market designs, the more severe the consequences of deficient token classification become.  The financial institution may be lulled into false assurance of reporting quality, even when actually misreporting, or applying controls that are inconsistent with the underlying token design.

Second, CARF moves reporting requirements upstream in tokenized asset processing. Recording tax residency, beneficial ownership, account or wallet linkage and transaction attribution can no longer be considered as after-thoughts in process design. They all must be embedded in onboarding, booking and lifecycle processes from the beginning. This is actually one of the reasons why tokenization should be considered to be a COO focus point, rather than merely a compliance-area one.

Third, CARF changes the economics of token asset distribution. The more fragmented the intermediation chain, the more difficult it becomes to preserve clean reporting obligations and a defensible data lineage. This fact will tend to favor operating models based on robust ‘source-of-truth’ data, and clear ownership of process governance and reporting tasks.

Fourth, asset tokenization will itself influence CARF implementation. As more conventional financial instruments acquire tokenized representations, tax authorities and regulators will face mounting pressure to clarify the reporting perimeter at the boundary between securities law, tax law and crypto-asset regulation. Japan’s interpretative treatment of on-chain transferable rights is an early example of this broader policy dynamic.

The strategic conclusion is that CARF will expose weaknesses in tokenized workflows in much the way that the T+0 roadmap will expose weaknesses in settlement workflows. Financial institutions that approach CARF as a narrow tax work stream will miss its deeper relevance to the future value of high-quality client data, operating design and product architecture.

Real-time collateral optimization

Real-time collateral optimization is one of the clearest economic cases for tokenization in banking. Banks manage large collateral pools across securities financing, derivatives, repo, prime brokerage and Lombard desks, and the potential economic value of improved outcomes is substantial. Tokenized collateral can reduce process frictions, lower excess buffers, improve substitution speed and support more efficient use of high-quality liquid assets.

The key operational shift is from static collateral allocation to continuous collateral orchestration. That requires banks to know, intraday, which assets are eligible where they are located, what they are pledged against, what haircuts apply and which counterparty obligations are coming due. In practice, this means that collateral optimization becomes inseparable from sourcing, pricing, custody and funding decisions. If one of those inputs are stale, the end-to-end result is sub-optimal – sometimes drastically so.

Recent market developments point in the same direction. The ECB has moved to accept tokenized securities as collateral in its liquidity and funding framework 3533, while US and wider industry initiatives around tokenized collateral and shared ledger infrastructures 36 are pushing towards 24x7 or near-real-time margining and transfer models. For banks, this means that collateral optimization is no longer simply about minimizing current-day funding costs, but more importantly about creating a system that can continuously re-rate the balance among liquidity, encumbrances and regulatory eligibility.

The executive question is therefore not whether tokenized collateral can improve efficiency. The real question is whether the bank can operationalize and robustly execute the controls required to make efficiency gains dependable under market stress. That requires not only technology, but also process governance over eligibility rules, intraday valuation, dispute handling, legal enforceability and backup settlement.

Implications across the products and services lifecycle

The impact of tokenization is most visible when viewed across the end-to-end operating lifecycle, rather than by sector (product or service) alone.

At issuance and onboarding, tokenization can reduce frictions in asset structuring, investor eligibility, transfer controls execution and settlement perfection. In an asset management context, this could materially improve transfer agent and distribution processes, provided token and mechanism designs are robust.

In trading and execution, tokenization becomes more valuable as market access extends. On-chain asset state machines can support better alignment among transaction controls, execution, servicing and surveillance, particularly where investor bases and liquidity are globally distributed.

For clearing, settlement and collateral management, the benefits of tokenization are strategically most consequential. This is also where compressed settlement cycles create the greatest need for synchronized ownership, liquidity, collateral and instructions data.

When it comes to asset servicing, mandate/fund administration and corporate actions, the value of tokenization stems from execution and traceability improvements.  These may be difficult to prioritize initially, as they depend on accurate synchronization (ideally by smart contract) across intermediation chains, and as tax and nominee structures may introduce local complexities. Tokenization can simplify parts of the synchronization tasks, but only if property rights, event logic and reporting obligations are represented on-chain consistently along the value chain.

For finance, risk and reporting, tokenization has the potential to drastically improve intraday visibility and thus reduce ambiguity of inputs to decisions. At the same time, it raises expectations around data governance, ledger reconciliation, third-party oversight, cyber resilience and tax transparency. In this sense, tokenization is both a compelling opportunity and a controls challenge.

It is a central thesis of this whitepaper that only an examination against the end-to-end business model of a bank or asset management company will generate the most compelling and durable enterprise value gains from asset tokenization. The industry direction is unmistakable and, in all probability, unstoppable, but it will be the wrong decision to focus only on token design and asset issuance before deciding on whether or not to follow the travel. The optimal operating point may not even be to create own tokenized assets, but rather to embed the tokenized paradigm into one’s own business model as a means to extract the highest possible business benefit from what will probably be a mandatory business capability in the future.

Implications by executive function

Chief Investment Officer

For the CIO, tokenization is relevant as it sits at the intersection of portfolio implementation, liquidity access, collateral usage and investment-product distribution. In a world moving towards faster settlement and more continuous trading, the CIO function increasingly has to think not only about expected return and risk profiles, but also about how assets behave operationally across trading venues, custodians, jurisdictions, and financing channels.

Two themes matter most. The first is cross-ledger interoperability. CIOs need assurance that tokenized positions can be represented consistently and move seamlessly across multiple networks without creating basis risk among the investment book, the custody records and collateral management. The second is real-time collateral optimization. For banks with trading, financing and prime brokerage activities, the ability to reuse high-quality collateral dynamically across positions is becoming a material balance-sheet and funding advantage.

The practical implication is that CIOs should assess tokenization through the lens of portfolio utility rather than technology novelty. Where tokenized assets improve value utility, financial optionality or collateral mobilization, they can enhance total portfolio efficiencies. Where they simply add operational complexity without improving efficiencies, then they should be treated as being simply a friction-minimizing option, not a strategic asset direction.

Chief Financial Officer

The CFO agenda begins with economics. Tokenization should be evaluated against measurable value pools: failed-trades reduction, lower reconciliation costs, reduced trapped collateral, faster and more certain cash cycles, improved collateral substitution (eventually, transformation), lower servicing frictions, and generally more efficient use of the balance sheet under shorter settlement windows. A robust finance-led tokenization business case should also capture loss avoidance: operational risk losses, client remediation expenses and liquidity inefficiencies that arise when financial institutions attempt to accelerate processes while still burdened with fragmented data and non-aligned control structures.

The most important CFO insight from the three afore-mentioned developments is that T+0 settlement is likely to re-price operational efficiency in the corporate value equation. In traditional settlement cycles, cost structure inefficiencies are often hidden within acceptable time buffers, handoff iterations and deferred exception handling. In compressed cycles, on the other hand, those same inefficiencies get magnified in the form of excess intraday liquidity demand, higher financing cost or failed client value monetization. Tokenization then becomes relevant, because it can safeguard financial outcomes by shifting focus from reactive/corrective to preventative controls.

Chief Operating Officer

The COO’s view deserves particular emphasis. Tokenization is, at its core, an operating model re-design problem. It changes where lifecycle ‘truth facts’ are created, who owns exceptions, how servicing obligations are discharged, and where control failures become commercially material. In the traditional world, many breaks can be identified after the fact and still be repaired through overnight workflows. In a T+0 or 24x5 world, on the other hand, unresolved temporary ambiguity has the potential to become a time-critical liquidity, client-servicing or conduct-risk issue.

This shift has major implications for operating designs. COOs will need to rethink process boundaries among front-office, middle-office, custody, treasury, tax operations, fund administration, mandate operations – and compliance throughout. They will need to re-design exception hierarchies, so that the most critical breaks are surfaced and resolved intraday – especially in ‘alert storm’ situations. They will also need to review outsourcing, service-center and global delivery models, because tokenized lifecycle events and CARF-related data obligations will increasingly require globally consistent 1st line of defense controls, rather than regionally coordinated (and sometimes improvised, due to lack of prior experience) exception handling.

Chief Risk Officer

For the CRO, tokenization matters because it changes the distribution of operational, liquidity, legal and model risks across the business landscape. The principal question is not whether tokenized assets are innovative, but rather whether the institution can evidence control over legal title, settlement finality, custody segregation, smart-contract dependencies, cross-ledger reconciliation and reporting classification under stress.

Tokenization can reduce certain risks by improving transparency and shortening time-to-finality, but it also introduces new risk vectors. For example, a tokenized operating model may concentrate threat and failure modes into key management, legal classification logic, interoperability layers, oracle inputs or shared infrastructure governance. Those risks create new dependencies across the tokenized and traditional financial worlds, which sit alongside old risk constellations and can amplify them if controls are not engineered appropriately.

From a CRO standpoint, the main objective is to preserve control effectiveness as the operating model becomes more accelerated and more distributed. That means reviewing whether existing risk appetite statements, 1st line of defense controls, operational resilience tests, outsourcing oversight, incident response playbooks and recovery procedures still hold when settlement timescales compress towards T+0 and when custody, collateral and reporting processes increasingly depend on synchronized digital state.

The CRO should also plan for cross-risk scenario testing in a ‘new world’ setting, so to speak, e.g. one that combines market risk with legal and on-chain operational risk stress factors. The critical test cases in a cross-ledger world are not only price shocks or volatility spikes, but also mis-classified tokens, smart contract bond-function inefficiencies, ledger outages, cross-jurisdiction service disruptions, wallet compromises, failed interoperability bridges, intraday margin calls/liquidations and cross-ledger tax reporting. In tokenized markets, resilience is not proven by considering average-day scenarios and estimated recovery time objective (RTO)/recovery point objective (RPO) metrics; it is rather proven when multiple dependencies are assumed to fail at once (in continuous, T+0 markets), and the institution can still evidence asset ownership/encumbrance, best execution and transaction finality controls.

Chief Technical Officer

For CTOs, the issue is not whether distributed ledger technology can be connected to, and within, the enterprise; it undisputably can. The harder question is whether the financial institution can create canonical asset and event models that span legacy and tokenized environments, while satisfying legal certainty, auditability, performance and resilience requirements. Without such common canonical models, tokenization risks becoming an additional layer of complexity and controls fragmentation rather than a cure for it.

This is particularly acute in hybrid, mostly independently evolving, legacy and tokenized environments, which will inevitably define the medium-term situation in the industry. Core, proven, transactional systems, books and records, custody platforms, treasury platforms, fund-accounting engines, transfer-agent workflow systems, tax and regulatory reporting systems will not be decommissioned because assets may transition to tokenized representations. The winning architectures will therefore be those that demonstrate robust interoperability and observability across infrastructures, starting from the proven existing ones, rather than targeting wholesale replacement prematurely.

Actions for executive committees

For financial institutions seeking a practical path forward, five actions should be prioritized over the next 12 to 24 months:

    

Define the enterprise thesis. Establish whether alignment with industry asset tokenization momentum should be pursued primarily for product innovation, post-trade efficiencies, distribution re-design, collateral mobility or market-infrastructure positioning. Without a clear thesis, tokenization activities will not progress past the pilot phase, as they will fail to prove any strategic value proposition.

    

Select jurisdiction(s) for rollout. The operating, tax and regulatory implications differ materially across potential client and asset domiciliation jurisdictions. Use-case selection must therefore be aligned with jurisdiction selection. Failure to do so will mask unforeseen risks and may result in tokenization investment reversal.

    

Build a target operating and data model (at least in reduced scope), before scaling. Asset classification, client identity spanning traditional and blockchain rails, asset domiciliation, property rights structuring within the token, ownership transfer logic, shadow liquidity and collateral management, tax parametrization, internal and external reporting obligations should be part of initial model design.

    

Treat T+0 and CARF as design inputs from the beginning. Settlement timescale compression and reporting transparency will soon be obligatory industry capabilities, not elective process choices. Thus, they should be treated as target-state requirements.

    

Re-design operating controls. Control points, exception ownership, intraday observability, third-party oversight, private key management, smart contract governance, end-to-end auditability should be designed to operate across the traditional and blockchain rails from the outset of tokenization implementation initiatives.

Closing perspective

The significance of DTCC’s 2025 tokenization initiative and LSEG’s 2026 LSE 24 announcement lies not in the narrow details of either. Their importance is that they jointly reveal where regulated financial market infrastructures are heading to: towards more continuous markets, more configurable assets and tighter coupling among product design, trading, settlement and post-trade operations.

This transition will not be linear, and it will not produce a fully on-chain financial system in the near term. The more probable outcome is a hybrid market architecture, in which incumbent infrastructures progressively adopt tokenized representations and programmable controls enabling improved efficiencies without compromising legal certainty or market integrity. That hybrid model is already emerging.

The financial institutions most likely to profit will not be those that tokenize the greatest number of instruments the fastest. They will rather be those that re-design their operating, data and controls models most effectively around the realities of 24x5 trading, compressed settlement times and global reporting transparency. For boards and executive committees, this is the moment to move from anticipation to design.

title: Is Your Institution Ready for What’s Next? Five Questions for Middle East Financial Services Leaders
snippet: As Middle East banks move beyond experimentation, leaders face important decisions about where to invest, what to scale and how to deliver value. Capco's regional experts examine five questions shaping the future of banking, spanning cross-border payments, sovereign cloud, Agentic AI, tokenization and wealth management
fullText:
Banks across the Middle East are operating in an environment shaped by rapid technological advancement, shifting customer expectations, geopolitical developments and growing resilience requirements. Financial institutions are balancing innovation with regulatory priorities while looking for new ways to improve efficiency, unlock growth and remain competitive. With many technologies now moving beyond the pilot stage, the focus is increasingly shifting from experimentation to scalable implementation and measurable business outcomes.
          

      

Against this backdrop, we see five themes shaping the banking agenda through 2026 and into 2027: the rise of Agentic AI and AI-enabled operating models; the evolution of cross-border payments and settlement infrastructure; the growing momentum behind tokenization and digital assets; the transformation of wealth management through personalization and changing client expectations; and the increasing importance of sovereign cloud as organizations prioritize resilience, control, and AI readiness. Together, these trends offer a view of how the region’s banks are preparing for the next phase of industry evolution.

How are cross-border payments moving from messaging to intelligent settlement?

Cross-border payments have long been a critical part of the Middle East banking landscape. As one of the world's largest remittance corridors, the GCC processes billions of dollars in outbound payments each year, making payment efficiency a strategic priority for regional banks.

For decades, international payments have relied on correspondent banking networks and messaging infrastructure that can introduce delays, reconciliation complexity and significant liquidity requirements. Banks often need to maintain funds across multiple currencies and jurisdictions to support payment flows, tying up capital and increasing operational costs.

In 2026, that model is beginning to evolve.

Driven by advances in blockchain-enabled settlement and modernization initiatives from established payment networks such as SWIFT, banks are exploring new ways to improve the efficiency of cross-border transactions. Traditionally, SWIFT's role has been to facilitate secure messaging between financial institutions. However, the industry is increasingly looking beyond messaging towards optimizing settlement itself through greater transparency, payment finality and improved liquidity management.

One of the most significant developments is the emergence of solutions that enable banks to net obligations across payment flows, optimizing liquidity usage and reducing the capital tied up in cross-border payments. For GCC banks, where remittances represent a major business line, this could significantly reduce one of the largest cost components of cross-border payments.

At the same time, newer settlement models promise faster reconciliation, improved payment tracking and greater visibility across the transaction lifecycle. Unlike earlier blockchain initiatives, many of these solutions are designed to work alongside existing payment infrastructure and standards, lowering implementation barriers and accelerating adoption.

Importantly, the market is now moving beyond experimentation. Documentation for new blockchain-enabled settlement frameworks was released in 2026, with industry pilot testing scheduled throughout the summer and initial go-live activity expected later in the year. This signals a shift from proof-of-concept discussions to practical implementation.

As customer expectations for speed and transparency continue to rise, banks are increasingly focused on reducing friction across the entire payment lifecycle. In 2026, the future of cross-border payments will be defined by smarter settlement, optimized liquidity and greater visibility across global payment flows.

How is sovereign cloud shaping the future of digital residency to digital resilience?

For years, cloud adoption in the Middle East was primarily driven by scalability, efficiency and cost optimization. Today, the conversation is evolving. As governments, financial institutions, energy companies and other critical industries become increasingly dependent on digital services, cloud is no longer viewed simply as a technology platform; it is becoming a core part of the region’s digital infrastructure.

Recent regional disruptions have reinforced an important reality: cloud services are supported by physical infrastructure, including data centers, connectivity networks and power systems. For organizations operating in highly regulated and business-critical sectors, resilience is becoming just as important as performance. Leaders are increasingly asking not only where their data resides, but how their operations can continue during periods of disruption.

At the same time, hyperscalers are adapting to these changing requirements. AWS, Microsoft and Google Cloud continue to expand their regional presence while introducing new capabilities around data control, encryption, local partnerships and sovereignty-focused operating models. These developments are helping organizations meet regulatory requirements while strengthening operational control and resilience.

However, sovereign cloud is no longer simply about selecting a local cloud region. Organizations are increasingly adopting a sovereign-by-design approach, embedding resilience, governance, security and operational control into cloud strategies from the outset. This means understanding where critical workloads sit, reducing concentration risk, strengthening access controls and ensuring services can recover quickly when disruptions occur.

The rise of AI is adding further momentum to this shift. As organizations look to deploy AI at scale, they must ensure sensitive data, models and workloads remain protected and aligned with local requirements. In many ways, sovereign cloud is becoming the foundation for the next wave of AI adoption, providing the trust, security and control needed to unlock greater value from data and AI initiatives.

Looking ahead, cloud strategy in the Middle East will be defined by more than migration and modernization. Organizations will increasingly focus on building digital environments that balance innovation with resilience, helping them maintain continuity, protect critical assets and support future growth. As this trend continues to evolve, organizations will need to translate sovereignty requirements into practical decisions around architecture, risk, governance and operating models.

How is AI Agents taking on banking operations? Balancing automation, governance and oversight

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase in financial services. After several years focused on GenAI tools that help employees search, summarize, analyze and generate content, attention is now turning to Agentic AI – systems capable of executing tasks and coordinating workflows while operating within defined controls and human oversight. For banks across the Middle East, this represents a significant shift.

Despite continued investment in digital transformation, many operational processes still rely heavily on human orchestration. Activities such as onboarding, KYC reviews, customer service, fraud monitoring and technology delivery often involve multiple handoffs, manual interventions and complex decision-making processes. Agentic AI offers an opportunity to streamline these activities by handling repetitive and structured tasks, allowing employees to focus on judgement-intensive work, customer interactions and exception management.

Rather than replacing people, the emerging model is one of collaboration, where AI agents perform specific activities while humans remain responsible for oversight, validation and decision-making. This is why many institutions begin with targeted use cases. Areas such as onboarding and KYC are particularly attractive because they rely on structured data, follow defined workflow and have clearly measurable outcomes.

Early experimentation is helping organizations understand where agentic systems can create value while also revealing the operational and governance requirements needed to support adoption at scale. As AI takes on a more active role in execution, governance is becoming a key differentiator. Institutions must look beyond traditional concerns such as data quality and model accuracy to address broader questions around accountability, auditability, control and the interaction between AI agents and human operators.

As a result, the conversation is increasingly shifting from technology to operating model design. The institutions that succeed will not necessarily be those deploying the most AI agents, but those that establish clear governance frameworks, define effective human-in-the-loop controls and build operating models that allow AI and people to work together safely and effectively.

Looking ahead, Agentic AI is likely to become a key enabler of productivity and scalability across banking operations. As organizations move from experimentation to adoption at scale, success will depend on establishing the right balance between automation, governance and human oversight.

How is tokenization moving from innovation to infrastructure?

The Middle East is rapidly establishing itself as a global hub for digital assets and tokenized finance. Supported by evolving regulatory frameworks, growing investment in financial market infrastructure and ambitious digital economy strategies, markets across the region are creating the foundations for tokenization to move beyond experimentation and into mainstream financial services.

The UAE has been at the forefront of this development, fostering regulated ecosystems where banks, exchanges, technology providers and regulators can collaborate to develop tokenized financial markets. Momentum is also broadening across the region. In Saudi Arabia, initiatives led by the Capital Market Authority (CMA) and Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) are supporting the modernization of capital markets, financial infrastructure and digital financial services. In Qatar, the Qatar Financial Centre (QFC) is helping develop the regulatory and institutional environment for digital assets, reinforcing the country’s wider ambitions around financial innovation and institutional capital.

Across these markets, institutions are expanding tokenized investment products, digital liquidity solutions and custody capabilities, while market infrastructure providers continue to strengthen the supporting ecosystem through advances in settlement, governance and shareholder servicing. Together, these developments are helping bridge the gap between distributed ledger technology and traditional financial markets, providing institutions with greater confidence to move from pilots toward scaled adoption.

For banks in the Middle East, the strategic question is no longer whether tokenization will become part of the financial landscape, but where to participate within the emerging ecosystem. Some institutions will focus on developing the infrastructure that supports tokenized markets, while others will prioritize client-facing services such as digital asset custody, tokenized investment products and wealth solutions. Many are likely to adopt hybrid approaches that combine infrastructure participation with new distribution and servicing capabilities.

Looking ahead, tokenization is expected to become an increasingly important component of the region's financial infrastructure. However, realizing its full potential will require more than adopting new technology. Banks will need interoperable platforms, robust governance, trusted digital custody and operating models that integrate tokenized assets seamlessly into existing banking and capital markets ecosystems.

How is wealth management shifting from product-led to relationship-led growth?

For decades, wealth management in the Middle East has been built on preserving and growing assets for high-net-worth clients. Today, that proposition is expanding. Rapid wealth creation, intergenerational wealth transfer and the emergence of regional financial hubs are reshaping client expectations, creating new opportunities for banks to deepen relationships while diversifying revenue beyond traditional banking services.

At the same time, the region is becoming an increasingly important destination for wealth itself. Financial centers such as Dubai and Abu Dhabi continue to strengthen their position as global wealth hubs, while Saudi Arabia’s significant concentration of high-net-worth and family office capital is being reinforced by regulatory reforms aimed at deepening its capital markets and investment ecosystem. Qatar adds another dimension, with its strong focus on sovereign capital deployment and a growing institutional family office landscape.

Together, these markets are attracting and retaining more capital through evolving regulation, sophisticated financial ecosystems and growing investor confidence. As more wealth remains within the region, banks have an opportunity to deliver locally while supporting increasingly global and sophisticated investment needs.

Client expectations are also evolving. A new generation of affluent customers expects seamless, personalized experiences that bring together banking, lending, investments and payments within a single relationship. Rather than viewing wealth management as a standalone business, leading institutions are integrating wealth propositions across the broader banking journey, using data and AI to provide more proactive advice, tailored investment strategies and deeper client engagement.

Technology is accelerating this transformation. AI-powered relationship management, intelligent portfolio insights, digital onboarding and automation are improving both advisor productivity and client experience, while emerging capabilities such as tokenized assets and digital custody are beginning to expand the range of investment opportunities available to sophisticated investors. Yet technology alone will not differentiate market leaders. Success will depend on combining digital innovation with trusted advisors, integrated client data and operating models that deliver personalized experiences at scale.

Looking ahead, wealth management in the Middle East will increasingly become a strategic growth engine rather than a specialist banking service. As competition intensifies, institutions that can build connected wealth ecosystems, bringing together advisory, investments, payments and lending into a seamless client experience will be best positioned to strengthen client loyalty, unlock new sources of fee income and capture the region's next phase of wealth creation.

How Capco can help

Turning emerging trends into competitive advantage requires more than technology adoption. It demands the right strategy, operating model and execution capabilities. Capco partners with financial institutions across the Middle East to help translate innovation into scalable business outcomes.

In cross-border payments, Capco supports banks in modernizing payment ecosystems, optimizing liquidity strategies and preparing for the next generation of settlement infrastructure as the industry moves toward smarter, more transparent payment models.

For organizations exploring Agentic AI, Capco helps identify high-value use cases, strengthen governance frameworks and scale adoption in a controlled and measurable way. Through Capco Smart Suite and its broader AI capabilities, firms can accelerate value realization while maintaining appropriate oversight and control.

In sovereign cloud, Capco supports clients in designing resilient cloud strategies, evaluating hyperscaler and partner ecosystems, strengthening governance and controls, and building the foundations required to scale both cloud and AI adoption with confidence.

Capco helps financial institutions define their digital asset strategy, assess opportunities across the tokenization value chain and develop the operating models, governance frameworks and technology capabilities required to support institutional adoption of tokenized assets.

In wealth management, Capco helps banks navigate the evolving wealth landscape by aligning operating models, digital capabilities and client engagement strategies with changing customer expectations.

Der digitale Euro: Die nächsten Schritte nach dem dritten Fortschrittsbericht der EZB

Trotz der Sommerpause gab es im Kontext des digitalen Euro erhebliche Bewegungen. Nach der Veröffentlichung des dritten Fortschrittsberichts der EZB im Juli 20251 haben zahlreiche Podiumsdiskussionen, Interviews und Stellungnahmen das Interesse und die Diskussion um eine europäische digitale Währung neu entfacht – und signalisieren, dass sich hinter der Einführung des digitalen Euro weiterhin positive Dynamik aufbaut.

Dieser aktuelle Bericht zeigt deutliche Fortschritte bei der Vorbereitung auf den Start des digitalen Euro. Die EZB wählt derzeit Anbieter für die digitale Euro-Plattform und -Infrastruktur aus und entwickelt zudem das Regelwerk mit Beiträgen der Rulebook Development Group. Technische Tests, einschließlich Offline-Funktionalität, werden durchgeführt, um eine praktische Nutzbarkeit sicherzustellen. Darüber hinaus bezieht die EZB verschiedene Interessengruppen wie kleine Händler und Verbrauchergruppen ein, um den digitalen Euro zugägnglich und benutzerfreundlich zu gestalten.

Die Vorbereitungsphase soll bis Ende 2025 abgeschlossen sein. Die endgültige Entscheidung über die Einführung des digitalen Euro wird jedoch erst getroffen, wenn der europäische Gesetzgebungsprozess Anfang 2026 abgeschlossen ist.

Warum besteht die Notwendigkeit eines digitalen Euro?

Laut der EZB ist der digitale Euro die Antwort auf die Fragen, die durch eine sich wandelnde Zahlungslandschaft und den Rückgang des Bargeldverbrauchs in der EU aufgeworfen werden. Da sich die Verbraucherpräferenzen* hin zu schnellen, bequemen und digitalen Zahlungsmethoden verlagern, gewährleistet der digitale Euro den Zugang zu Zentralbankgeld in einem Format, das diesen modernen Anforderungen entspricht. Demnach schließt der digitale Euro die Lücke zwischen Bargeld und digitalen Zahlungsmethoden.

Er ist als Ergänzung zum Bargeld konzipiert und ermöglicht sowohl Online- als auch Offline-Transaktionen in gleichem Maße. Gleichzeitig erfüllt er die gleichen Anforderungen an Sicherheit und Privatsphäre wie Bargeld. Dies unterscheidet den digitalen Euro von den heute gängigen Zahlungsmethoden, die mit einer Abhängigkeit von Geschäftsbanken, Zahlungsdienstleistern oder Kryptoanbietern verbunden sind und nicht das gleiche Maß an Stabilität, Zugang oder Privatsphäre bieten.

Über die Bedürfnisse der Verbraucher hinaus spielt er auch bei der Bewahrung der monetären Souveränität und der Aufrechterhaltung finanzieller Stabilität eine entscheidende Rolle, indem er die Autorität der Zentralbank über öffentliches Geld angesichts des Aufstiegs privater Alternativen sichert. Der digitale Euro zielt darauf ab, die strategische Autonomie der EU zu stärken, indem die Abhängigkeit von nicht-europäischen Zahlungssystemen reduziert und eine größere Kontrolle über die Finanzinfrastruktur gewährleistet wird. Durch das Angebot einer einheitlichen, sicheren und effizienten Lösung soll er nahtlose, paneuropäische Zahlungen ermöglichen und die Integration im gesamten Euroraum fördern. Damit folgt die EU dem globalen Trend, bei dem 134 Länder – die 98 % des globalen BIP repräsentieren – die digitale Zentralbankwährung (CBDCs) erforschen und elf Länder bereits ihre eigene CBDC eingeführt haben. In Europa begann die Arbeit am digitalen Euro 2020 mit der Explorationsphase, gefolgt von der Untersuchungsphase von 2021 bis 2023. 2025 markiert das Ende der Vorbereitung, in der die EZB die technische Nutzbarkeit, regulatorische Compliance und harmonisierte Umsetzung im gesamten Euroraum definieren will.

Im Kern dieses Bemühens steht das Regelwerk für das digitale Euro-System, das einen standardisierten Rahmen für Zahlungsdienstleister bietet, um Konsistenz, Innovation und Interoperabilität bei digitalen Euro-Diensten sicherzustellen und einen Prototyp zu entwickeln.2

Der digitale Euro wird von der N€XT-Abrechnungsmaschine angetrieben. Der Unterschied zwischen N€XT und traditionellen Abwicklungssystemen besteht darin, dass traditionelle Systeme Buchungslogik verwenden und Kontosalden führen, während N€XT ein Modell auf Basis von Unspent Transaction Output (UTXO) verwendet. Dieses ist von der Blockchain-Technologie inspiriert, bei dem jede Transaktion erfasst und verfolgt wird. Zudem wird eine Microservice-Architektur genutzt, um schnelle, skalierbare und private Transaktionen zu ermöglichen.

Der Prototyp der EZB testete sowohl Online-Zahlungen (z. B. E-Commerce, P2P) als auch Offline-Zahlungen. Offline-Nutzung auf sicherer Hardware (z. B. JavaCard) ermöglicht eine Abrechnung ohne Unabhängigkeitsprüfung. Obwohl das System gute Leistung und Integration zeigte, sind weitere Arbeiten nötig, um Sicherheits- und Skalierbarkeitsziele zu erreichen – insbesondere für den Offline-Einsatz.

Das folgende Diagramm illustriert diese Architektur, mit N€XT im Kern und Anwendungsfällen, die über das Regelwerk für das digitale Euro-System verbunden sind.3

Auf regulatorischer Ebene steht der digitale Euro im Einklang mit bestehenden gesetzlichen Regelungen wie PSD2, DORA und dem Vorschlag zur digitalen Euro-Regulierung. Risikomanagement-Rahmenwerke wurden vorgeschlagen, um Betrug, Cyberrisiken und Abhängigkeit von Drittanbietern zu bekämpfen. Zahlungsdienstleister müssen zertifiziert sein, um sicherzustellen, dass sie die Regeln einhalten und sicher starten.

Ebenso wichtig für die Regulierung ist der Schutz der Privatsphäre. Das Design der EZB verhindert die Nachverfolgung von Nutzersalden oder Zahlungsmustern durch das Eurosystem. Darüber hinaus erlauben auf Transaktionen basierende Prüfmechanismen datenschutzfreundliche Zahlungen, insbesondere bei Transaktionen mit geringem Wert, innerhalb der regulatorischen Grenzen.

Auswirkungen auf Marktakteure

Während die Vorbereitungsphase andauert, ist eines klar: Der digitale Euro wird Kernakteure im Finanzdienstleistungs-, Handels- und öffentlichen Sektor beeinflussen. Für Banken und Zahlungsdienstleister (PSPs) wird die bedeutendste Änderung die Neudefinition ihrer Rolle als Vermittler sein. Im Zuge der Einführung des digitalen Euro sind die Institute verpflichtet, digitale Euro-Geldbörsen für ihre Kunden bereitzustellen und zu verwalten und so den Zugang zu zentralbankgestütztem Geld zu gewähren. 

Um einen reibungslosen Betrieb zu gewährleisten, müssen sie auch die Infrastrukturbereitschaft sicherstellen und die Abwicklungsschicht der EZB mit ihren bestehenden Frontend-Systemen integrieren. Dies wird erhebliche technische Anpassungen erfordern, um die Kompatibilität mit dem neuen digitalen Währungsrahmen zu gewährleisten. Gleichzeitig werden die Compliance-Aufgaben zunehmen, da Banken und PSPs komplexe regulatorische Anforderungen bewältigen müssen, darunter Anti Money Laundring (AML)-Verpflichtungen, Datenschutz, Reservierungsgrenzen und verschiedene Berichtspflichten.

Für Händler und Einzelhändler wird der digitale Euro erhebliche Aufrüstungen ihrer Kassen- (POS) und Kassensysteme erfordern. Diese Systeme müssen neue Formen digitaler Euro-Transaktionen unterstützen, darunter QR-Codes, NFC-Zahlungen und möglicherweise Offline-Zahlungsoptionen, um die Kompatibilität mit der sich wandelnden Zahlungslandschaft sicherzustellen.

Darüber hinaus könnte sich das Kostenmodell für Händler zu ihren Gunsten verschieben, da der digitale Euro niedrigere Transaktionsgebühren als traditionelle Kartensysteme bieten und so möglicherweise die Kosten für die Zahlungsabwicklung senken könnte. Wie bei anderen Akteuren im Ökosystem müssen Händler diese technischen und finanziellen Anpassungen bewältigen und sich gleichzeitig an das neue regulatorische Umfeld rund um digitale Währungen anpassen.

Vorbereitung auf den digitalen Euro: Was die Marktakteure jetzt tun müssen

Da sich das digitale Euro-Ökosystem weiterentwickelt, erfordert eine erfolgreiche Umsetzung eine strikte Einhaltung gesetzlicher Vorschriften sowie strategische Koordination über Technologie, Betrieb und Governance. Im Folgenden stellen wir die vier Schwerpunktbereiche fest, die Marktteilnehmer ansprechen müssen, um sich auf den digitalen Euro vorzubereiten.

1. Gesetzliche und regulatorische Anforderungen

    

Überwachen und analysieren Sie EU- und EZB-Vorschriften (z. B. DSGVO, PSD2/3, AMLD5/6, DORA).

    

Durchführung von Compliance-Gap-Bewertungen zwischen internen Richtlinien und regulatorischen Anforderungen.

    

Passen Sie AML-/KYC-Prozesse für digitale Euro-Wallets an.

2. Operational Business Process Readiness

    

Entwickeln Sie Zahlungsflüsse für P2P-, POS- und E-Commerce-Transaktionen.

    

Richten Sie Abstimmungsprozesse mit der digital Euro-Settlement-Platform (DESP) ein.

    

Stellen Sie die Einhaltung der ISO 20022-Zahlungsstandards für Transaktionsformate und Messaging sicher.

3. Technische Infrastruktur & Integration

    

Führen Sie technische Gap-Analysen und Architekturüberprüfungen in Kernbanken, Middleware, Mobil-/POS- und DESP-Schnittstellen durch.

    

Optimieren Sie API-Gateways und Middleware für Skalierbarkeit, Resilienz und Überwachung.

    

Verwalten Sie Zertifizierungs- und Testprogrammen für Systeme und Geräte.

    

Stellen Sie sicher, dass Systeme ISO 20022-konforme Transaktionsmessaging und Datenaustausch unterstützen.

4. Risiko- und Betrugskontrollen

    

Abbildung der EZB-Betrugstaxonomie auf interne Risiko- und Betrugskontrollrahmen.

    

Integration mit der EZB-Risk & Fraud Management (RFM)-Plattform.

    

Implementieren Sie Geolokalisierung und Verhaltensanomalienerkennung, um Betrug zu verhindern.

Zentrale Erkenntnisse und Ausblick

Der dritte Fortschrittsbericht zum digitalen Euro zeigte deutliche Fortschritte bei der Vorbereitung auf die Markteinführung. Laut EZB stellt der digitale Euro ein modernes, flexibles Zahlungssystem dar, das Innovation mit traditionellen Methoden verbindet und die EU auf die sich wandelnde digitale Zahlungslandschaft vorbereitet. Die EZB wählt Plattformanbieter aus, entwickelt das Regelwerk und testet technische Funktionalitäten, einschließlich Offline-Zahlungen, um die Benutzerfreundlichkeit sicherzustellen. Die Einbindung der Interessengruppen sorgt dafür, dass der digitale Euro zugänglich und benutzerfreundlich ist, während Bargeld weiterhin zentral im Zahlungssystem bleibt. Aus dieser Sicht ergänzt der digitale Euro Bargeld und stärkt die finanzielle Souveränität der EU, indem er eine sichere, gesamteuropäische digitale Zahlungslösung bereitstellt.

Banken, PSPs und Händler müssen ihre Systeme anpassen, Zahlungsflüsse verbessern und neue regulatorische Anforderungen erfüllen. The digital euro is the first digital central bank currency in the euro area. As a state-guaranteed, digital means of payment, it complements cash and existing payment instruments and is intended to be used throughout Europe, both online and offline.

For banks, payment service providers, merchants and other market participants, this means much more than just another regulatory requirement. The digital euro will influence existing payment transaction architectures, customer interfaces and value chains . Institutions are faced with the task of interpreting regulatory requirements and integrating the digital euro into their business and operating models strategically.

Our range of service

Capco and Wipro provide financial institutions and companies with holistic support on their way to the digital euro integration. We combine regulatory expertise, in-depth payment transaction know-how and extensive transformation experience with strong technological implementation expertise.

Together, we support the introduction of the digital euro from the initial classification and the development of viable target models through to technical implementation and operation of effective solutions. The focus is on strategic relevance, regulatory compliance and operational efficiency.

What to do now

    

  

    

        

          

          

  Selection of suitable partners and solutions 

          

        

        

          

            Not all requirements relating to the digital euro have to be implemented by  the firm. From connection to the Digital Euro Service Platform (DESP), wallet solutions to reporting and reconciliation processes, the selection of suitable partners and ready-made solutions is a key success factor for efficient and scalable implementation.          

        

      

    

        

          

          

  Conception and target architecture 

          

        

        

          

            The regulatory requirements for the digital euro must be translated into concrete business and technical requirements at an early stage. As part of a gap analysis, existing payment transaction architectures must be evaluated, necessary extensions identified and an integrated target state developed. The aim is an efficient and sustainable integration of the digital euro into existing processes and systems. In some cases, this may also require the definition and implementation of a fundamentally new payment transaction target models.          

        

      

    

        

          

          

  Impact analysis on business model and organization 

          

        

        

          

            The digital euro has an impact on existing products, processes and responsibilities. These effects should be analyzed at an early stage in order to minimize risks and exploit opportunities in a targeted manner. At the same time, adjustments in governance, organization and operating model are to be expected, and must be actively shaped.
